text:
Given: Iteration rule: X_{k+1}=1.5X_k-0.5X_kX_k^T X_k., Concrete initial matrix: X_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.8\end{bmatrix}., The initial singular values are 1.2 and 0.8., The scalar singular-value update is f(\sigma)=1.5\sigma-0.5\sigma^3., The initial singular values lie in the interval (0,\sqrt{3}), where this example converges toward 1.
Find: The successive matrices X_k, their singular values, and the limiting orthogonal matrix.

1. Interpret the iteration as a matrix product
   Xₖ₊₁=1.5Xₖ-0.5XₖXₖᵀXₖ
   The expression X_k(X_k^TX_k) means first compute X_k^TX_k and then multiply X_k on the left. Therefore the cubic matrix term is X_kX_k^TX_k. This is the form used in every animation frame.

2. Choose a concrete matrix whose entries are easy to display
   X₀=begin bmatrix1.2&0\\0&0.8end bmatrix
   Use a diagonal matrix so that each matrix product can be shown numerically and each diagonal entry can be tracked independently. Its singular values are the absolute values of its diagonal entries, so the initial singular values are 1.2 and 0.8.

3. Compute the first Gram matrix
   X₀ᵀX₀=begin bmatrix1.2&0\\0&0.8end bmatrixbegin bmatrix1.2&0\\0&0.8end bmatrix=begin bmatrix1.44&0\\0&0.64end bmatrix
   Because X_0 is diagonal and symmetric, X_0^T=X_0. The squared diagonal values are 1.2^2=1.44 and 0.8^2=0.64. In the visualization, show this as a second heatmap or labeled matrix grid.

4. Compute the cubic matrix term
   X₀X₀ᵀX₀=begin bmatrix1.2&0\\0&0.8end bmatrixbegin bmatrix1.44&0\\0&0.64end bmatrix=begin bmatrix1.728&0\\0&0.512end bmatrix
   Multiplying the matrices from Steps 2 and 3 gives diagonal entries 1.2(1.44)=1.728 and 0.8(0.64)=0.512. This is the cubic term that is subtracted in the update.

5. Form the first updated matrix
   X₁=1.5begin bmatrix1.2&0\\0&0.8end bmatrix-0.5begin bmatrix1.728&0\\0&0.512end bmatrix=begin bmatrix0.936&0\\0&0.944end bmatrix
   Scale the original matrix by 1.5, scale the cubic term by 0.5, and subtract entry by entry. The first diagonal update is 1.5(1.2)-0.5(1.728)=0.936. The second is 1.5(0.8)-0.5(0.512)=0.944. Animate the two diagonal entries moving from 1.2 and 0.8 toward 1.

6. Derive the singular-value transformation
   Xₖ=UΣₖVᵀ Longrightarrow XₖXₖᵀXₖ=UΣₖ³Vᵀ Longrightarrow Xₖ₊₁=U (1.5Σₖ-0.5Σₖ³ )Vᵀ
   Write a singular-value decomposition X_k=U\Sigma_kV^T, where U and V are orthogonal. Since V^TV=I and U^TU=I, the cubic product preserves the same singular vectors and cubes each singular value. Therefore each singular value evolves independently according to f(\sigma)=1.5\sigma-0.5\sigma^3.

7. Track the two singular values numerically
   σ₁,₁=1.5(1.2)-0.5(1.2)³=0.936, σ₂,₁=1.5(0.8)-0.5(0.8)³=0.944
   The singular values of X_1 are 0.936 and 0.944. Applying the scalar rule again gives \sigma_{1,2}=1.5(0.936)-0.5(0.936)^3=0.993987072 and \sigma_{2,2}=1.5(0.944)-0.5(0.944)^3=0.995383808.

8. Continue the iteration and prepare the line graph
   begin arrayc|cck&σ₁,ₖ&σ₂,ₖ\\hline 0&1.2&0.8\\1&0.936&0.944\\2&0.993987072&0.995383808\\3&0.9999458757449175&0.999968085340874\\4&0.9999999956059267&0.9999999984721981\\5&1.0&1.0end array
   Plot iteration number k horizontally and the two singular values vertically. The graph should show both curves approaching the horizontal level 1. The first singular value initially decreases because it starts above 1, while the second increases because it starts below 1.

9. Explain why the fixed singular value is 1
   f(1)=1.5(1)-0.5(1)³=1
   The value 1 is a fixed point of the singular-value map. The derivative is f'(\sigma)=1.5-1.5\sigma^2, so f'(1)=0. This means the linear error term vanishes near 1, explaining the rapid improvement visible in the line graph.

10. Identify the limiting orthogonal matrix
   Xₖ→ I₂=begin bmatrix1&0\\0&1end bmatrix, I₂ᵀI₂=I₂
   For the chosen diagonal example, both singular values converge to 1 while the singular vectors remain unchanged. Thus X_k converges to the identity matrix. Since the identity satisfies I_2^TI_2=I_2, the limiting matrix is orthogonal.

11. State the general matrix conclusion
   boxed σₖ₊₁=1.5σₖ-0.5σₖ³, Xₖ₊₁=1.5Xₖ-0.5XₖXₖᵀXₖ, Xₖ→ UVᵀ
   The iteration keeps the singular-vector factors U and V and applies the scalar map to every singular value. When all singular values converge to 1, the diagonal singular-value matrix converges to I, so X_k=U\Sigma_kV^T converges to UV^T, which is orthogonal because (UV^T)^T(UV^T)=VU^TUV^T=I.

Answer: boxed σₖ₊₁=1.5σₖ-0.5σₖ³, Xₖ₊₁=1.5Xₖ-0.5XₖXₖᵀXₖ, Xₖ→ UVᵀ
Use X_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.8\end{bmatrix}. The iteration produces X_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.936&0\\0&0.944\end{bmatrix}, then singular values (0.993987072,0.995383808), then values increasingly close to (1,1). In general, the singular values are updated independently by \sigma\mapsto1.5\sigma-0.5\sigma^3. When they converge to 1, the matrix converges to UV^T, an orthogonal matrix; for this diagonal example, UV^T=I_2.

11 steps, 11 slides — 2 step(s) sympy could not prove — 82% of slides draw a figure Illustrated 6 slide(s).

operations.title: Read the Update
operations.caption: X_{k+1}=1.5X_k-0.5X_kX_k^TX_k
operations.narration: First form the Gram matrix X_k transpose X_k, then multiply it on the left by X_k. That makes the cubic term X_k X_k transpose X_k.

operations.title: Choose X_0
operations.caption: X_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.2&0\\0&0.8\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: We choose a diagonal starting matrix. Its diagonal entries, and therefore its singular values, are 1.2 and 0.8.

operations.title: Form the Gram Matrix
operations.caption: X_0^TX_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.44&0\\0&0.64\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: The matrix is diagonal and symmetric, so its transpose is itself. Squaring the diagonal entries gives 1.44 and 0.64.

operations.title: Build the Cubic Term
operations.caption: X_0X_0^TX_0=\begin{bmatrix}1.728&0\\0&0.512\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: Multiplying X_0 by the Gram matrix once more produces the cubic diagonal values 1.728 and 0.512.

operations.title: Make the First Update
operations.caption: X_1=\begin{bmatrix}0.936&0\\0&0.944\end{bmatrix}
operations.narration: Scale X_0 by 1.5, subtract half of the cubic term, and obtain X_1. Both diagonal values move closer to 1.

operations.title: What the SVD Reveals
operations.caption: X_k=U\Sigma_kV^T\Longrightarrow X_kX_k^TX_k=U\Sigma_k^3V^T
operations.narration: The SVD shows that the singular vectors U and V stay fixed. Each singular value is transformed independently by the same cubic scalar rule.

operations.title: Track Two Singular Values
operations.caption: \sigma_{k+1}=1.5\sigma_k-0.5\sigma_k^3
operations.narration: The value starting above 1 decreases, while the value starting below 1 increases. After two updates they are both already near 1.

operations.title: Convergence to One
operations.caption: \sigma_{1,k},\sigma_{2,k}\to1
operations.narration: Continuing the iteration, both singular values rapidly approach 1. By iteration 4 the remaining error is tiny, and the displayed values round to 1 by iteration 5.

operations.title: Why One Is Special
operations.caption: f(\sigma)=1.5\sigma-0.5\sigma^3,\quad f(1)=1,\quad f'(1)=0
operations.narration: One is a fixed point because f of 1 equals 1. Also, the derivative at 1 is zero, so the linear error term disappears and convergence accelerates.

operations.title: The Orthogonal Limit
operations.caption: X_k\to I_2,\qquad I_2^TI_2=I_2
operations.narration: For this diagonal example, the singular vectors remain unchanged, so the matrix approaches the identity. The identity is orthogonal because its transpose times itself is the identity.

operations.title: Final Answer
operations.caption: \boxed{\sigma_{k+1}=1.5\sigma_k-0.5\sigma_k^3,\qquad X_{k+1}=1.5X_k-0.5X_kX_k^TX_k,\qquad X_k\to UV^T}
operations.narration: In general, every singular value follows the cubic scalar map. When they all converge to 1, the matrix converges to U V transpose, an orthogonal matrix; here that limit is the identity.
